Restore
rē-stōr´
v. (to bring back to a former and better state; to make good what was lost, broken or taken)
Latin restaurare, to rebuild, renew. The Hebrew shub behind most Old Testament uses is the same verb rendered repent — a turning back — which is why restoration and repentance are so often the same movement seen from two sides.

Biblical Definition

To restore is to bring back what was lost. God does it to a soul: “He restoreth my soul: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name's sake” (Psa 23:3). David asks for it after a great fall, and notice what he asks for: “Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation” (Psa 51:12) — the joy, not the salvation. God promises it to a ruined nation: “I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten” (Joe 2:25). The church is commanded to do it to a fallen brother: “restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted” (Gal 6:1). And it is the shape of the end: “the times of restitution of all things” (Act 3:21).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines restore as to return to a former place or state; to bring back; to repair; to recover from injury; to heal; and to bring back or recover from lapse, degeneracy, doubts or errors.

expand to see more

RESTORE, v.t. To return to a former place or state; to bring or send back.

2. To repair; to rebuild.

3. To heal; to cure; to recover from disease; as, to restore health.

4. To make restitution or satisfaction for a thing taken.

5. To recover from lapse, degeneracy, declension or ruin; as, to restore one to the favor of God.

Key Scripture

Psa 23:3 — "He restoreth my soul: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name's sake."

Psa 51:12 — "Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation; and uphold me with thy free spirit."

Joe 2:25 — "And I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten, the cankerworm, and the caterpiller, and the palmerworm, my great army which I sent among you."

Gal 6:1 — "Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted."

Act 3:21 — "Whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things, which God hath spoken by the mouth of all his holy prophets since the world began."

Modern Corruption

Restoration is treated as forgiveness alone, and Scripture attaches to it a specific manner, a specific warning, and often a bill.

expand to see more

Galatians 6:1 is the most practical verse in the New Testament on restoring a fallen brother, and every clause is load-bearing. It is addressed to ye which are spiritual, which disqualifies the eager. The verb is the one used for setting a broken bone and for mending nets — slow, skilled work, not a pronouncement. It specifies the manner: in the spirit of meekness. And it ends with the clause the restorer needs most: considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted. A man who approaches a fallen brother without that sentence running in his head will do damage, however correct his doctrine.

Psalm 51:12 is exact about what sin costs a believer and what it does not. David does not ask to be restored to salvation; he asks for the restoration of its joy, and for a right spirit to be renewed within him. That distinction has kept many a Christian from despair after a serious fall and has kept many another from presumption, since the loss is real and severe even where the standing is secure. What sin takes from a believer is the enjoyment of what he still has.

Joel 2:25 is the promise people cling to and it should be quoted whole, because the years are restored by the God who names the locusts as my great army which I sent among you. The devastation was judgment, not accident. That is what makes the promise worth anything: the One restoring is the One who took it away, and He does not restore by pretending the ruin did not happen. Acts 3:21 puts the same logic at the end of history — the times of restitution of all things — which is not a return to Eden but something further on, a creation delivered from the bondage of corruption.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shub (H7725), to turn, restore; shalam (H7999), to make whole, repay; Greek katartizo (G2675), to mend, set in order; apokatastasis (G605), restitution.

expand to see more

Hebrew shub (H7725) — to bring back, restore; Psalm 23:3, 51:12, Joel 2:25, Isaiah 1:26.

Greek katartizo (G2675) — to mend, restore, set a bone; Galatians 6:1, Matthew 4:21, 1 Thessalonians 3:10, Hebrews 13:21.

Greek apokatastasis (G605) — restitution, restoration; Acts 3:21 only.

Usage

"“He restoreth my soul” — and then leadeth, in the same verse."

"“Considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted” — the clause the restorer needs."

"“The years that the locust hath eaten” — and He had sent them."
